subject: Cloud Computing
title: Cloud Repatriation: Coming Home
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Cloud Repatriation: Coming Home.

hook.text: 37signals moved off the cloud and saved $7 million over five years. Is leaving the cloud the new trend?

buildup.text: At scale, cloud can be more expensive than owned hardware. Some companies are moving workloads back on-premises.

discovery.text: Repatriation makes sense for stable, predictable workloads. Bursty, unpredictable work still belongs in the cloud.

twist.text: Most companies aren't going all-in or all-out. They're finding the right mix: cloud for some things, owned for others.

climax.text: The debate isn't cloud versus on-premises. It's which workloads belong where. The answer is different for every company.

punchline.text: Some left the cloud. Most stay. The right answer varies.

quiz.question: When does cloud repatriation make financial sense?
options: For stable, predictable workloads where owned hardware costs less at scale
It always makes sense to leave the cloud immediately
Only when a company has fewer than 10 employees

details.summary: Some organizations are moving workloads from public cloud back to owned infrastructure, a trend called cloud repatriation. Companies like Dropbox and Basecamp found that at their scale, owned hardware costs less. However, repatriation suits specific workloads, not a wholesale cloud rejection.
details.whyItMatters: Repatriation challenges the assumption that cloud is always the answer. For certain workloads at certain scales, owned infrastructure is genuinely more cost-effective.
takeaways: Some companies save millions by moving workloads off cloud
Repatriation works best for stable, predictable workloads
Most organizations still find cloud more cost-effective overall

faq.question: When does cloud repatriation make sense?
faq.answer: Repatriation is typically viable for large-scale, stable workloads with predictable resource needs. Dropbox saved tens of millions by moving storage off S3. However, the operational cost of running your own infrastructure including hiring, maintenance, and upgrades must be factored in.

faq.question: Is cloud repatriation a trend?
faq.answer: Repatriation happens but is not a broad trend. For every company leaving the cloud, many more are migrating to it. The most common pattern is hybrid: keeping variable workloads in the cloud while repatriating specific high-volume, stable workloads to owned hardware.
